title: A Galaxy Telescope Accidentally Found a Brand-New Comet
summary:
A telescope built to photograph distant galaxies has spotted something much closer to home: a brand-new comet. The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope captured it in images taken between September 16 and 24, 2026 — the first comet the mission has ever discovered.

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery. His software flagged a streak smeared across several images — the mark of a fast-moving object. Predicting where it would appear next, he found it in five sets of images, and a fuzzy cloud around it showed it was an active comet shedding dust and gas.

The comet appeared in a region called the Euclid Deep Field North. After checking catalogs of known asteroids and comets, Pöntinen reported it to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center, which officially confirmed the discovery on October 8. The comet is now called C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

The comet sits about 1.3 billion kilometers (about 800 million miles) from Earth — about as far as the Sun is from a point between Jupiter's and Saturn's orbits. But it travels well outside the flat plane in which the planets orbit the Sun, almost directly above it, on a path that will take thousands of years to complete.

Finding comets is not Euclid's job. Euclid avoids the sky around the plane of the solar system, where dust makes light that could interfere with its pictures of the distant universe, and it photographs each section of the sky only once. 'Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid,' says Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, 'so it was a happy coincidence' that the comet's orbit and Euclid's scanning lined up.

The find also gives scientists practice for ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission, showing how teams could work together to spot future targets.
why_it_matters: A lucky find like this shows how space telescopes can surprise scientists, and it helps teams prepare to chase future comets up close.

background_read: A comet is a chunk of ice, dust, and rock that orbits the Sun, and when it nears the Sun it sheds dust and gas that form a fuzzy cloud around it.
Telescopes in space take pictures of the sky to study faraway objects such as galaxies, huge groups of stars held together by gravity.
Because a moving comet leaves a streak across several pictures, scientists can spot one by comparing images taken at different times.
When someone thinks they have found a new comet, they report it so other scientists can check it and give it an official name.
